sources.title: 33a - The Scythians
sources.note: T. Sulimirski and T. Taylor, chapter Summary and metadata, pages 547 to 590: archaeological traces before names, sixth-century core-periphery complexity, nomadism as one element, trade, fortified centers, and power by 500 BCE.

sources.title: A Chronology of the Scythian Antiquities of Eurasia Based on New Archaeological and 14C Data
sources.note: Radiocarbon 43(2B), pages 1085 to 1107, especially pages 1085 to 1087: beginnings vary regionally; the authors distinguish a combined pre-Scythian and initial epoch, an early epoch, and a classical epoch.

sources.title: New Burials of the Pre-Scythian Time From the North-Eastern Azov Area
sources.note: Article abstract, paragraphs 1 to 5: excavated early Iron Age burials precede Scythian-time sites; Chernogorivka, Novocherkassk, and Cimmerian attributions are author interpretations.

sources.title: Settlement System of the Dnieper Left-Bank Forest-Steppe of the Second Half of 8th - Middle of 6th Centuries BCE
sources.note: Article abstract and citation, pages 91 to 100: agricultural settlements, ashhill clusters, shared necropoleis, nomadic groups, routes, wintering, interaction, and interpretive limits.

sources.title: Re-evaluating Scythian Lifeways: Isotopic Analysis of Diet and Mobility in Iron Age Ukraine
sources.note: Peer-reviewed article, abstract, Materials and Methods, Results, and Conclusions: human isotope samples, local mobility, varied diets, urban locales, and rejection of a homogeneous nomadic model.

sources.title: Social Stratification of the Population of the Forest-Steppe Area of the Dnieperland During the Early Scythian Period
sources.note: Marcin Burghardt, Sprawozdania Archeologiczne 69 (2017), pages 133 to 183; pages 133 to 140 methods and sample, 159 to 173 interpretation and limits.

sources.title: Mound 1/2021 of the Skorobir Necropolis in the District of Bilsk Gorodyshche
sources.note: Article abstract: first-quarter sixth-century BCE female burial, wooden grave architecture, pottery, glass and rock-crystal beads, gold plaques, local elite interpretation, and ancient looting.

sources.title: Barrow of the Scythian Period near Malynivtsi Village in Podillya
sources.note: Article abstract: late seventh to first-half sixth-century BCE inhumation and cremation, scattered human remains, jewelry, seventeen vessels, nearby settlement, and ordinary-community interpretation.

sources.title: Scythian female warriors in the south of Eastern Europe
sources.note: Elena Fialko, Folia Praehistorica Posnaniensia 22, pages 29 to 47; abstract and printed pages 42 to 43: total date range, earliest graves in the second half of the seventh to beginning of the sixth century BCE, and main concentration in the fourth century BCE.

sources.title: On the Eve of the “Scythian Invasion” to Central Europe: a New Warrior Grave in Bilsk
sources.note: Article abstract: Barrow 1/2020 dated 580/570 to 560/550 BCE, handmade pottery, two iron bits, spearhead, quiver and arrowheads; campaign link is an interpretation.

sources.title: Early Scythian Quiver Sets of the First Half of the 6th Century BC in the South of Eastern Europe
sources.note: Article abstract: quiver sets dated with Greek transport and painted amphorae; listed burial complexes span Kuban to Dnieper forest-steppe and illustrate wide connections.

sources.title: Copper Wrought Cauldron of the Early Scythian Period from the Vicinity of Bilsk Fortified Hillfort
sources.note: Article abstract, paragraphs 1 to 8: first-half sixth-century BCE find, morphology and X-ray fluorescence analysis, central Caucasian production connection, Urartian handle influence, and cautious mobility hypothesis.

sources.title: Scherban A. Spinning and Weaving among the Population of the Left-Bank Forest-Steppe of the Ukraine of the Seventh - Early Third Centuries BC (on the Basis of Ceramic Materials)
sources.note: National Academy thesis record, abstract and bibliographic fields: ceramic evidence, spindle whorls, vertical and horizontal looms, domestic manufacture, and broad seventh to early-third-century scope.

sources.title: Processes of Early Iron Age Urbanisation of Eastern European Forest-Steppe: The State of the Art
sources.note: Article abstract and PDF pages 5 to 24, especially pages 12 to 19: fortifications, production, trade, ritual, settlement clusters, metalworking techniques, labor, and uncertainty.

sources.title: On the Issue of the Architecture of Defensive Structures of the Eastern Fortification of Bilsk Hillfort
sources.note: Article abstract: open settlements from late eighth century, light boundaries by third quarter sixth century, later ramparts and moat, distinct traditions, and changing defenses.

sources.title: Cocklebur in the Archaeological Chronicle of Ukraine
sources.note: Article abstract, Scythian-period paragraph: three finds including Bilsk, two clay impressions, isolated evidence, and later medicinal use that cannot be back-projected.

sources.title: Diet and Oral Health of Scythian Populations in Ukraine (700-200 BCE): Evidence for Grain Consumption and Food Processing
sources.note: International Journal of Osteoarchaeology 2026 article, abstract and Results: 36 individuals from Bilsk, Medvin, and Mamai-Gora; caries, calculus, abscesses, tooth loss, wear, and sample limits.

sources.title: Paleo-proteomic analysis of Iron Age dental calculus provides direct evidence of Scythian reliance on ruminant dairy
sources.note: Pecnik et al., PLOS One 2026, abstract, Methods, Results, and figure captions: milk proteins in calculus from two Ukrainian Iron Age populations; direct dietary evidence with site and sample limits.

sources.title: The Population of the Forest-Steppe Zone of Ukraine During the Scythian Time
sources.note: Article abstract, paragraphs 1 to 8: craniological series, non-homogeneous forest-steppe population, difference from steppe samples, and bias because cremations leave no comparable remains.

sources.title: Genetic history of Scythia
sources.note: Andreeva et al., Science Advances 2025, Results and Discussion: temporally and geographically distinct communities were genetically heterogeneous; shared cultural elements do not establish one ethnicity. The linked article records a 27 March 2026 erratum and states that its conclusions are unaffected.

sources.title: Royal marriage alliances and noble hostages
sources.note: Karen Radner, Assyrian Empire Builders, University College London and ORACC, section Assyrian princesses marrying abroad: Esarhaddon, Bartatua, contemplated treaty and marriage, and exact reference SAA 4 20.

sources.title: Introducing the Scythians
sources.note: British Museum overview sections on evidence, mobility, wagons, horses, craft, and archaeology; examples span wide regions and dates, so comparisons remain labeled.

sources.title: Scythians, ice mummies and burial mounds
sources.note: St John Simpson, British Museum, sections on burial mounds and society: cemeteries, mound scale, preservation, grave goods, family grouping, and limits of mortuary evidence.

sources.title: Defining an indicator package to allow identification of ‘cesspits’ in the archaeological record
sources.note: David N. Smith, Journal of Archaeological Science 40 (2013), printed pages 526 to 527 and Table 1: 49 features at 11 British sites, dating from the late eleventh to late sixteenth century CE with most from the twelfth to fifteenth centuries; a comparative identification method, not evidence from the atlas region.

sources.title: Harness or bridle fitting
sources.note: Metropolitan Museum of Art object 61.60.1, Artwork Details: circa seventh to sixth century BCE, Eurasian steppes, bronze, dimensions, and catalog attribution “Scythian (?)” retaining uncertainty.

sources.title: Expanding the Corpus of the Earliest Scythian Animal-Style Artefacts
sources.note: Antiquity article, opening and Tunnug 1 context: 833 to 800 BCE dating, early animal-style corpus, human and horse sacrifice, and distant Inner Asian scope.

sources.title: On Relations Between Scythians and Greeks in North Coast of Black Sea
sources.note: Maryna V. Skrzhynska, article keywords and abstract: wider Archaic and Classical named-Scythian evidence, Greek-speaking and writing interpreters, wine, tableware, expensive arms, Greek goldsmiths, and poor mutual understanding; some described activity is explicitly fifth-century BCE.

sources.title: Glass Beads from Burial and Household Contexts of the Bilsk Hillfort in the Dnipro Forest-Steppe (Late 7th to 4th Century BC)
sources.note: Stanislav Zadnikov, Arts 15(8), 2026, abstract and Introduction, plus section 3.1 and Figure 3: dated settlement and burial contexts, dugouts, household pits, ash hills, Greek ceramics, and exchange limits.

sources.title: Scythian Language
sources.note: Rüdiger Schmitt, Encyclopaedia Iranica, opening paragraphs 1 to 3: no authentic continuous Scythian texts; evidence is indirect and fragmentary, chiefly names recorded by Assyrian, Persian, and Greek neighbors; dialect diversity remains unresolved.
